  "importance_rationale": "This is an author-declared open question from Marvian, Lidar and Hen (arXiv:1802.03408), stated verbatim in the paper's 'Conclusions and open questions' section and restated by the candidate without strengthening or narrowing. It is a named-paper open question but not a famous named problem, so no authoritative-formulation mismatch arises. The candidate correctly isolates the first of the source's two listed open questions (constant-depth circuits with two-body rotations) from the second (reducing locality to 2-local), which is handled as a separate candidate. Importance is medium rather than high: the question is a genuine, explicitly flagged extension whose answer determines whether the paper's NP-completeness barrier to curing the sign problem is an artifact of restricted single-qubit transformation classes or a robust feature of richer, more physically motivated circuit classes, but it is one technical branch of the broader computational-stoquasticity program rather than the central question of that program.",
  "scientific_significance_score": 6,
  "scientific_significance_rationale": "Solving this would settle a complexity bound for a richer and more physically relevant transformation class than the single-qubit Clifford/orthogonal classes for which NP-completeness is proven. Concretely: (1) knowledge — it would tell the quantum Monte Carlo community whether seeking curing transformations under constant-depth circuits with two-qubit rotations is NP-hard (guiding researchers away from exhaustive search) or tractable (opening a new algorithmic route to sign-problem-free formulations); (2) capability — a polynomial-time algorithm would directly become a practical pre-processing tool for QMC simulations of fermionic and frustrated quantum systems; (3) mechanism — either outcome clarifies whether two-body entangling rotations fundamentally change the complexity landscape of stoquasticity conversion, connecting to the known fact that two-qubit gates suffice to escape the single-qubit obstructions. It would change research decisions about which curing strategies to invest in, but it does not by itself resolve the practical sign problem or the 2-local and approximate-curing variants.",
  "expected_result": "A correct final submission is a complexity classification of the exact decision problem the source poses: deciding whether a local Hamiltonian admits a curing transformation (into stoquastic, sign-problem-free form) under constant-depth quantum circuits that may include two-qubit rotations, discrete or continuous. Acceptable forms, matching the answer types the question naturally commits to: (a) a membership and/or hardness result placing the problem in a named complexity class (e.g., an NP-completeness proof via rigorous reduction, or containment in some class with matching hardness); (b) a polynomial-time algorithm that decides or finds such curing transformations, accompanied by a correctness proof and runtime analysis; or (c) a rigorous conditional-hardness or impossibility result. The submission must address the stated transformation class including two-body rotations — discrete, continuous, or both with explicit treatment of which case is settled — and must not silently revert to single-qubit-only transformations, since that is the already-resolved case.",
  "answer_types": [
    "proof",
    "construction",
    "counterexample"
  ],
  "verification_clarity": "clear",
  "verification_standard": "A submission passes if and only if it provides a mathematically rigorous complexity classification of the stated decision problem for the stated transformation class. Branch by answer type: (1) hardness/membership claim — a reduction is given from (or to) a known complete problem with every step of the reduction verified, membership in the claimed class demonstrated, and the reduction shown to produce exactly the curing instances for constant-depth circuits allowing two-qubit rotations; (2) algorithm claim — a concrete algorithm is exhibited with a proof that it correctly decides (or finds a witness for) curability under the stated circuit class and a proof of the claimed runtime bound; (3) impossibility/conditional claim — the assumption is named explicitly and the derivation from that assumption is rigorous. In all branches the reviewer checks that the transformation class in the argument genuinely includes two-body rotations (stating whether the discrete, continuous, or both variants are covered), that the problem being classified is the existence/decision problem for curing transformations as in the source, and that no hidden restriction to single-qubit transformations or to a fixed finite gate set beyond the source's framing has been introduced.",
  "decomposition_parent_coverage": "not_applicable",
  "proposed_subproblems": [],
  "verification_difficulty": 5,
  "verification_difficulty_rationale": "The acceptance condition is a complexity classification, so no branch of the contract is settled by a finite witness, mechanical check, replay, or certificate; all branches are derivation review (mode D). The result genuinely answers the source question because the source explicitly asks for the computational complexity of exactly this decision problem, and a classification with rigorous argument is the complete answer. The cheapest sound branch is likely a hardness proof via reduction or an algorithm with a correctness proof; either way the reviewer must reconstruct connected reasoning whose steps depend on one another: in the hardness branch, correctness of the gadget construction under two-body rotations, faithfulness of the reduction, and membership arguments; in the algorithm branch, the invariant/correctness argument and runtime bound. These are connected multi-step derivations but use standard complexity-theoretic technique rather than a long, fragile, or novel chain, placing the residual in the 4-6 band; 5 reflects a moderately deep reduction or correctness argument plus the explicit check that the argument covers two-body rotations rather than reverting to the resolved single-qubit classes. Specification fidelity is near-trivial (the decision problem and transformation class are pinned by the source statement) and is not counted as extra residual. Limits that remain for the reviewer: confirming the discrete-versus-continuous coverage claimed, and confirming that the input encoding (local Hamiltonian description, circuit depth bound) matches the source framing.",
